# The Exercises and Professional Competencies {#sec-appendix-competencies}

This appendix maps the book's exercises, comprehensive cases, and capstone cases to the competency areas of four frameworks that accounting programs use to plan courses and to document what their students learn. It is written for instructors who align a course with the CPA Evolution model curriculum, with the management accounting competencies of the Institute of Management Accountants (IMA), with the International Education Standards of the International Federation of Accountants (IFAC), or with the accounting accreditation standards of AACSB International. An entry means that the item practices the competency as one of its main tasks, not that it covers everything the framework expects. Each item is mapped to at most three competencies in each framework, the ones its requirements exercise most directly.

The tables use short labels. A number such as 6.5 is Exercise 6.5, B.1 is an exercise of [the appendix on publishing, securing, and sharing reports](#sec-appendix-publishing), and C.1 one of [the appendix on Power BI in the browser](#sec-appendix-browser). Part II R5 is Requirement 5 of the comprehensive case that closes Part II, and Ch. 19 R4 is Requirement 4 of the capstone case in Chapter 19. Every exercise and requirement in the book appears at least once in each table.


## The Frameworks

The CPA Evolution model curriculum of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) and the National Association of State Boards of Accountancy (NASBA) describes what accounting programs can teach to prepare candidates for the CPA Exam (AICPA & NASBA, 2021). Its core covers accounting and data analytics, audit and accounting information systems, and tax, and three disciplines build on it. @tbl-d-01 uses the curriculum's own structure: Core S1 is the core section on accounting and data analytics, Core S2 the core section on audit and accounting information systems, BAR the business analysis and reporting discipline, and ISC the information systems and controls discipline, each followed by the module (M) and, where it matters, the topic (T).

IMA's expanded management accounting competency framework organizes the competencies of management accountants into ten domains, each with embedded competencies described at three proficiency tiers: foundational, proficient, and expert (IMA, 2025). @tbl-d-02 lists the domains and competencies that the book practices. It leaves the tier to the instructor, because the same item can be assigned at different depths.

IFAC's International Education Standards set out the competence that professional accountants develop in their initial professional development. Revised versions, issued in 2025, take effect in July 2026: IES 2 sets out the areas of technical competence, IES 3 the professional skills, and IES 4 the professional values, ethics, and attitudes (IFAC, 2025a, 2025b, 2025c). @tbl-d-03 uses the standards' area letters, such as IES 2 (i) for information and communications technologies, and paraphrases their learning outcomes.

AACSB International's standards for accounting accreditation include Standard A5, Digital Agility. It expects the curriculum to integrate the technologies of accounting practice, students to judge whether a technology fits a task and to interpret and communicate its results, and students to learn new technologies as the profession changes (AACSB International, 2026). @tbl-d-04 maps the items to the standard's three parts, with Part 5.1 divided by the tool each item uses.


## Using the Map

The tables work in two directions. To choose assignments, start from a competency that the course must cover and pick from the items in its row. To document a course, start from the items the course assigns and collect the rows in which they appear. The solutions on the [Downloads](#sec-downloads) page give the expected results of every item, which helps when an item serves as evidence of what students learned.

For the AACSB table that lists each course's technologies, describe the Excel work as Power Query, data models, and analysis tools rather than as spreadsheet use, because Standard A5 leaves ordinary productivity software out of that table (AACSB International, 2026). The SQL and Power BI work fits the table as it is.

The frameworks change more often than the exercises do. IFAC's standards were revised in 2025 and AACSB's accounting standards in 2026, so check the current version of a framework before relying on a code from these tables.
